---
title: "Expanded and arrival matrices"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("setup.R")
```

`travel_time_matrix()` reduces the trips of a departure window to a few
percentiles. Two functions keep the trips themselves:
`expanded_travel_time_matrix()` returns every one, and
`arrival_travel_time_matrix()` the one that leaves latest and still arrives in
time. Both work with public transport (`mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT")`).

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "Left: the expanded matrix has one row per departure minute and draw for each pair, with the breakdown of the trip. Right: the arrival matrix scans departures from the latest minute back and keeps the first trip that arrives by the arrival time."}
fig("expanded-arrival.svg")
```

## Every trip

```{r}
trips <- expanded_travel_time_matrix(
  network, points[1:2, ], points,
  mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = departure,
  time_window = 3,
  breakdown = TRUE,
  seed = 42,
  n_threads = 2
)
nrow(trips) == 2 * nrow(points) * 3 * 5
head(subset(trips, routes != "[WALK]"), 10)
```

A row is one departure minute of one origin-destination pair. This feed is
frequency-based, so each minute has `draws_per_minute` rows (5 by default),
one per simulated schedule; with a timetable-based feed there is one row per
minute. Within a minute the draws are **sorted by total time** and numbered,
so `draw_number` is a rank (1 is the fastest draw), not the order in which the
draws were made.

With `breakdown = TRUE` each trip is split into minutes of `access_time`
(walk to the first stop), `wait_time`, `ride_time`, `transfer_time` (walks
between vehicles) and `egress_time`, plus the `routes` taken (GTFS
`route_id`s joined by `|`, or `[WALK]` for a trip on foot) and `n_rides`.
Every time is in minutes with one decimal, and `total_time` is the sum of the
rounded parts:

```{r}
t <- subset(trips, routes != "[WALK]")[1, ]
with(t, c(sum = access_time + wait_time + ride_time + transfer_time + egress_time,
          total_time = total_time))
```

Trips longer than `max_trip_duration` keep their row with `NA` times.

## The latest trip that arrives in time

`arrival_travel_time_matrix()` takes an `arrival_datetime` instead of a
departure. As r5r does, it searches departures minute by minute over the
`max_trip_duration` minutes before the arrival (the window may start on the
previous day) and, for each pair, keeps the first trip, from the latest
departure backwards, that arrives by the arrival time.

```{r}
arrive <- arrival_travel_time_matrix(
  network, points[1:2, ], points,
  mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  arrival_datetime = as.POSIXct("2019-05-13 15:00:00", tz = "America/Sao_Paulo"),
  max_trip_duration = 30,
  breakdown = TRUE,
  seed = 42,
  n_threads = 2
)
head(arrive)
```

There is at most one row per pair; pairs that cannot arrive in time are
absent.

## Limits

r5r computes these matrices with R5's path bookkeeping, which refuses more
than 5,000 destinations; peabiru keeps the same limit. The expanded matrix
grows with origins × destinations × minutes × draws, so it is meant for a
few origins at a time.
